cards: Latin is the language of ancient Rome, which spread across the western Mediterranean with Roman rule and became the root of the Romance languages.
Slavery is the condition in which people are treated as property and forced to work.
The ivory trade is the commerce in elephant tusks, prized for carving and luxury goods.
A mercenary is a soldier who fights for pay in the service of a foreign power.
A sugar plantation is a large agricultural estate growing sugarcane for sugar production, typically using intensive labour.
A manuscript is a handwritten book or document.
A census is an official count of a population, often recording households, property and obligations.
The Atlantic slave trade was the forced transportation of millions of enslaved Africans to the Americas between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries.
A guild is an association of craftsmen or merchants practising the same trade, organised to regulate production, training and standards and to protect members' interests.
Coffee is a drink made from the roasted seeds of the coffee plant, originally from Ethiopia and Yemen, which spread through the Islamic world and then Europe.
The fur trade was the commerce in animal pelts, highly valued for clothing and as luxury goods.
Guerrilla warfare is a form of irregular warfare in which small, mobile forces use raids, ambushes and knowledge of terrain against larger conventional armies.
Sanskrit is a classical Indo-Aryan language of South Asia, used for religious, literary, philosophical and scientific texts over more than three millennia.
Printing is the mechanical reproduction of text and images.
A war elephant is an elephant trained for combat, used to charge enemy formations, carry archers and intimidate opponents.
Caravan trade is long-distance overland commerce carried by groups of merchants with pack animals, typically camels, travelling together for safety.
A constitutional monarchy is a form of government in which a monarch is head of state but exercises power within the limits of a constitution.
The spice trade was the long-distance commerce in spices such as pepper, cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg from South and Southeast Asia.
A chariot is a light, two-wheeled, horse-drawn vehicle used in warfare, carrying a driver and an archer or spearman.
Hebrew is a Semitic language, the language of the Hebrew Bible and of ancient Israel.
A mounted archer is a cavalry soldier who shoots arrows from horseback.
Piracy is robbery and violence committed at sea.
The musket is a muzzle-loading, smoothbore firearm that became the standard infantry weapon in many armies from the sixteenth to the nineteenth century.
Field artillery refers to mobile cannon used on the battlefield.
The Silk Road was the network of overland trade routes linking China with Central Asia, Iran, the Middle East and the Mediterranean.
Serfdom was a form of unfree labour in which peasants were bound to the land and owed labour or dues to a lord.
Aramaic is a Semitic language that became the common language of much of the Near East in the first millennium BCE.
Deportation refers to the forced removal of people from their homes to other places.
A naval blockade is the use of warships to stop shipping from reaching or leaving an enemy's ports.
Pastoralism is a way of life based on herding livestock such as cattle, sheep, goats, horses and camels, often involving seasonal movement between pastures.
Cuneiform is a writing system of wedge-shaped signs pressed into clay tablets, invented in Mesopotamia in the late fourth millennium BCE.
Gunpowder is an explosive mixture of saltpetre, charcoal and sulphur, first developed in China.
Porcelain is a fine, hard, translucent ceramic first developed in China.
Smallpox is a highly contagious viral disease that was a leading cause of death in many societies until its eradication in 1980.
Kannada is a Dravidian language spoken mainly in the Indian state of Karnataka, with more than 40 million speakers.
An entrepôt is a port or trading centre where goods are imported, stored and re-exported, often without further processing.
A galley is a warship propelled mainly by oars, dominant in Mediterranean warfare for centuries.
Jihad is an Islamic term meaning struggle or striving, which can refer to spiritual effort or to armed struggle in defence or expansion of the faith.
Caste refers to a system of hereditary social groups, often tied to occupation and restricting marriage between groups.
Conscription is compulsory enlistment of people into state service, especially the armed forces.
Genocide is the deliberate destruction of a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
Heavy cavalry refers to mounted troops with substantial armour and weapons, used for shock action against enemy formations.
A eunuch is a castrated man, and in many courts eunuchs served as palace officials, guards of the royal household and administrators.
Papyrus is a writing material made from the pith of the papyrus plant, which grew abundantly in the Nile valley and delta.
A subsidy is a payment made by a state to support another party.
Maharaja ('great king') is a Sanskrit royal title used across South Asia, originally for major sovereigns and later by many Hindu and Sikh rulers of princely states.
Slave raiding is the capture of people by force to be enslaved and sold or used for labour.
Inflation is a sustained rise in the general level of prices, reducing the purchasing power of money.
The telegraph was a system for transmitting messages over long distances by electrical signals along wires, developed in the nineteenth century.
Urdu is an Indo-Aryan language closely related to Hindi, written in a Perso-Arabic script and rich in Persian and Arabic vocabulary.
A customs union is an agreement among territories to remove tariffs between them and adopt a common external tariff.
Syriac is a dialect of Aramaic that became the main literary and liturgical language of many Christian communities in the Near East from the early centuries CE.
The trans-Saharan trade was the network of caravan routes across the Sahara Desert linking North Africa and the Mediterranean with West and Central Africa.
Prakrit is the name for the vernacular Middle Indo-Aryan languages of ancient India, related to Sanskrit but simpler in sound and grammar.
The cowrie shell is the shell of a small sea snail, used as currency across Africa and Asia.
An amphora is a two-handled ceramic jar used in the ancient Mediterranean world to transport and store goods such as wine and olive oil.
A reservoir is an artificial or enlarged body of water used to store water for irrigation, drinking or flood control.
A caravanserai is a roadside inn built around a courtyard, providing lodging for travellers and their animals along trade routes in the Islamic world.
Indian Ocean trade refers to the maritime exchange of goods such as spices, textiles, gold, ivory and ceramics across the Indian Ocean, driven by seasonal monsoon winds.
Middle Persian, also called Pahlavi, was the Iranian language of the Sasanian Empire, descended from Old Persian and ancestral to modern Persian.
Siege warfare is the conduct of military operations to capture or defend fortified places, through blockade, assault, mining or bombardment.
Calligraphy is the art of decorative handwriting, highly developed in the Islamic world, where it adorned manuscripts, buildings and objects.
Nahuatl is a Uto-Aztecan language spoken by the Mexica and other peoples of central Mexico.
Arabic is a Semitic language that spread with Islam from the Arabian Peninsula across the Middle East and North Africa.
The Greek language is an Indo-European language with a written history stretching back over three thousand years.
A lingua franca is a language used for communication between speakers of different native languages.
The monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds that brings heavy summer rains to South and South-East Asia.
The gold trade refers to the commerce in West African gold, often exchanged for Saharan salt and carried across the desert to North Africa and the Mediterranean.
A phalanx is a dense formation of heavily armed infantry fighting in close ranks.
Rajpramukh was the title of the head of a union of former princely states in the Republic of India between 1948 and 1956, an office comparable to a state governor.
Akkadian is an extinct Semitic language of ancient Mesopotamia, written in cuneiform.
A composite bow is a bow made from layers of wood, horn and sinew glued together, giving great power in a short length suitable for use on horseback.
Feudalism is a term for systems in which land was granted in return for military service and loyalty, creating hierarchies of lords and vassals.
The matchlock was an early firearm mechanism in which a slow-burning match was lowered onto the priming powder to fire the gun.
The dirham was the silver coin of the Islamic world.
A hill fort is a fortification built on high ground, using the natural terrain for defence.
Horse breeding is the raising of horses for transport, warfare and trade.
Iron working is the craft of smelting and forging iron to make tools and weapons.
Universal suffrage is the right of all adult citizens to vote, regardless of property, class or, in its full form, sex.
The Warring States period was the final phase of the Eastern Zhou in ancient China, when seven major states, Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Han, Zhao and Wei, fought for supremacy.
Linear B is the syllabic script used by the Mycenaean palaces of Greece and Crete from about 1450 to 1200 BCE to record an early form of Greek.
Sanctions are penalties, usually economic, imposed by states or international bodies to pressure another state to change its behaviour.
A bazaar is a market or commercial quarter, typically of covered streets, shops and workshops, found in cities across the Islamic world and South Asia.
English is a Germanic language that originated in England.
The salt trade refers to the long-distance exchange of salt, a vital commodity for human diet and food preservation.
Oscan was an Italic language spoken in southern Italy by the Samnites, Campanians, Lucanians and related peoples in the second half of the first millennium BCE.
Ostrich feathers were a luxury trade good valued for decoration and fashion, carried north from the Sahel and Sahara across trans-Saharan routes.
Quechua is a family of languages spoken by some eight to ten million people in the Andes, chiefly in Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador.
A Bantustan, or homeland, was a territory set aside for Black South Africans of a particular ethnic group under apartheid.
Corvée labour is unpaid work required by a state from its subjects, often for building and maintaining public works or for military service.
Land tenure refers to the rules and arrangements by which land is held, used, granted and transferred.
An obelisk is a tall, narrow, tapering stone monument, often carved from a single block.
Paper money is currency printed on paper rather than minted in metal.
Savannah is a type of tropical grassland with scattered trees, found widely across Africa between the rainforest and the desert.
A concentration camp is a place where large numbers of civilians or prisoners are detained, usually without trial, in harsh conditions.
Deforestation is the large-scale clearing of forests.
A galleon was a large, multi-decked sailing ship used from the sixteenth century for war and long-distance trade.
Lacquerware is objects coated with lacquer made from the sap of the lacquer tree, producing a durable, glossy finish.
Nayaka, meaning leader or chief, was a title for military commanders in medieval South India.
The Phoenician alphabet is a script of 22 consonant letters, written from right to left, used in Phoenicia and across the Mediterranean for most of the 1st millennium BCE.
Syiem is the title of the chief of a traditional Khasi state, or hima, in the hills of present-day Meghalaya, India.
A crossbow is a bow mounted horizontally on a stock, shot by a trigger mechanism, allowing troops with limited training to shoot powerful bolts.
A hoplite was a heavily armed Greek infantryman, equipped with a large round shield, spear and armour, fighting in the close formation known as the phalanx.

The Indo-European languages are a family of related languages spoken across Europe and much of western and southern Asia, descended from a reconstructed ancestor, Proto-Indo-European, probably spoken in the 4th millennium BCE.
The Semitic languages are a family of languages of the Near East and North Africa that includes Akkadian, Aramaic, Hebrew, Phoenician, Arabic and Ge'ez.
Telugu is a Dravidian language of south-eastern India, the main language of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana and one of the most widely spoken languages of India.
Cartography is the science and art of making maps.
Grand Duke of Tuscany was the title created by Pope Pius V in 1569 for Cosimo I de' Medici, ruler of Florence and Siena, and confirmed by the emperor in 1576.
Linear A is the undeciphered script used by the Minoans of Crete for administration and religious inscriptions from about 1800 to 1450 BCE.
Marathi is an Indo-Aryan language spoken mainly in western India, in present-day Maharashtra.
Primogeniture is the rule of inheritance by which the eldest son succeeds to the whole of a title or estate.
A ziggurat is a massive stepped temple tower built in ancient Mesopotamia and Elam, with a shrine on its summit.

The Berber languages, also called Tamazight, are a branch of the Afroasiatic family spoken by the Amazigh peoples of North Africa, from Morocco and Algeria to Libya, Egypt's Siwa Oasis and the Tuareg regions of the Sahara and Sahel.
A cohort was a tactical unit of the Roman army, normally about 480 men, with ten cohorts forming a legion.
A horse archer is a mounted warrior who shoots with a bow from horseback, combining mobility with missile firepower.
Khalifa, rendered in English as caliph, is the Arabic title for the successor to the Prophet Muhammad as leader of the Muslim community.
Shirvanshah, "king of Shirvan", was the title of the rulers of Shirvan in the eastern Caucasus.
A siege engine is a device designed to break or bypass fortifications, such as a battering ram, siege tower, catapult or trebuchet.

Afrikaans is a West Germanic language that developed at the Cape of Good Hope from the Dutch spoken by settlers of the Dutch East India Company, with influence from Malay, Portuguese, Khoekhoe and other languages.
French is a Romance language that developed from Latin in France.
The Kabaka of Buganda is the title of the king of Buganda, the largest of the traditional kingdoms in present-day Uganda.
Persian miniature is a tradition of small, detailed painting, usually used to illustrate manuscripts of poetry and history.
Sapa Inca, the 'unique Inca', was the title of the ruler of the Inca state.
The sarissa was a very long pike, several metres in length, carried by the infantry of the Macedonian phalanx.
The Early Bronze Age is the first phase of the Bronze Age in the Near East and the Aegean, roughly 3300 to 2000 BCE.
A gymnasium was a Greek institution for physical training and education, which also served as a centre of social and intellectual life.
The hajj is the pilgrimage to Mecca that every Muslim who is able is expected to make at least once in a lifetime, one of the five pillars of Islam.
Russification was the policy of spreading the Russian language, culture and administration among the non-Russian peoples of the Russian Empire and later the Soviet Union.
The arquebus was an early form of matchlock firearm used from the fifteenth to the seventeenth century.
A brigade is a military formation made up of several battalions or regiments, smaller than a division.
Carolingian minuscule is a clear, legible script developed in the late eighth century in the Carolingian Empire.
The Columbian Exchange is the transfer of plants, animals, diseases and people between the Americas and the rest of the world following Columbus's voyages from 1492.
A cupbearer was a court official who served drinks to the king, a position of trust and access to the ruler.
The denarius was the standard silver coin of the Roman Empire for several centuries.
Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system of ancient Egypt, using pictorial signs for sounds and words.
Greek fire was an incendiary weapon used by the Byzantine Empire, typically projected from siphons on warships, and able to burn on water.
A huerta is an irrigated agricultural area in Spain, especially around Valencia, Murcia and Granada, using irrigation channels developed in the Islamic period.
Khwarazmshah ('Shah of Khwarazm') was the title of the rulers of Khwarazm, the oasis region on the lower Amu Darya south of the Aral Sea.
The Meroitic script was the writing system of the Kingdom of Kush in its Meroitic period, used from about the second century BCE.

The Secretary-General of the United Nations is the chief administrative officer of the United Nations and head of its Secretariat, appointed by the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council, usually for five-year terms.
A steamship is a ship powered by a steam engine.
Synthetic dyes are colourants produced by industrial chemistry rather than extracted from plants or animals, a technology that developed rapidly from the mid-nineteenth century.
U-boat is the English name for German military submarines, from the German Unterseeboot.
Wet-rice agriculture is the cultivation of rice in flooded paddy fields, a highly productive system that can support dense populations.
Yiddish is a language of the Ashkenazi Jews, based on medieval German with Hebrew, Aramaic and Slavic elements and written in the Hebrew alphabet.
Attrition refers to a form of warfare in which victory depends on wearing down the enemy's manpower and material resources through continuous losses.
A bombard is a large early cannon, usually a muzzle-loader firing heavy stone balls, used mainly in sieges in the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries.

The British Overseas Territories are the fourteen territories under British sovereignty that are not part of the United Kingdom, mostly small islands left from the British Empire, such as Gibraltar, the Falkland Islands, Montserrat and…
The Cis-Sutlej states were the Sikh and other states of the Malwa region of Punjab between the Sutlej and Yamuna rivers, among them Patiala, Nabha and Jind.
El Niño is the periodic warming of surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific, part of a climate cycle that recurs every few years.
German Emperor was the title of the head of the German Empire from 1871 to 1918, always held by the King of Prussia.
Jury trial is a legal procedure in which a panel of citizens decides the facts of a case.
Old Persian is the ancient Iranian language of the Achaemenid kings, written in a cuneiform script.
Partible inheritance is a custom by which a father's property is divided among all his sons rather than passing to a single heir.
Pashto is an Eastern Iranian language spoken by the Pashtuns of Afghanistan and north-western Pakistan, written in a modified Arabic script.
Prince of Wales was the title claimed by native Welsh rulers of Gwynedd as overlords of Wales.
Romansh is a Romance language spoken in the canton of Graubünden in eastern Switzerland, descended from the Latin of the Roman province of Raetia.
Sericulture is the raising of silkworms for the production of raw silk, typically by feeding them on mulberry leaves.
Total war is warfare in which states mobilise their entire population, economy and resources, and in which the distinction between combatants and civilians is eroded.
Tyrian purple is a deep purple dye produced from murex sea snails, named after the Phoenician city of Tyre.

The Yang di-Pertuan Agong is the head of state of Malaysia, a constitutional monarch elected for a five-year term by the Conference of Rulers from among the nine hereditary rulers of the Malay states.
Ashura is the tenth day of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar.
A breech-loading rifle is a firearm loaded at the rear of the barrel rather than through the muzzle, allowing much faster reloading, especially when lying down.
A catapult is a siege engine that hurls projectiles using tension, torsion or human traction, used before gunpowder artillery.
Hangul is the Korean alphabet, created in 1443 under King Sejong of Joseon and promulgated in 1446 as the Hunminjeongeum, "the proper sounds for instructing the people".
Kshatriya is the second of the four varnas of the traditional Hindu social order, the class of rulers and warriors, ranked after the Brahmins.
The Malay language is an Austronesian language spoken in the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and much of maritime South-East Asia.
Measles is a highly contagious viral disease.
Passover is a major Jewish festival commemorating the Exodus of the Israelites from Egypt, celebrated in spring from the 15th day of the month of Nisan.
The Pythia was the priestess of Apollo at Delphi who spoke the god's oracles.
The Saka era is a calendar era beginning in 78 CE, used widely in India and in Hindu-Buddhist Java and Bali to date inscriptions and chronicles.
A spirit medium is a person believed to be possessed by and speak for ancestral or other spirits.
Tuʻi Kanokupolu is the title of the third and youngest of Tonga's royal lines, founded in the early 17th century by a son of the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua.
The West Indies Associated States was the collective name for British colonies in the eastern Caribbean that became states in free association with the United Kingdom under the West Indies Act 1967.
Aerial bombardment is the use of aircraft to drop bombs or other munitions on military or civilian targets.
An agora was the central public space of an ancient Greek city, used for markets, assemblies and civic life.
An aquifer is an underground layer of rock or sediment that holds water.
The Attic standard was the weight standard for silver coinage originating in Athens, based on a tetradrachm of about 17 grams.
A battering ram is a siege weapon consisting of a heavy beam used to break down gates and walls.
Brazilwood is a tropical tree whose dense red heartwood was valued in early modern Europe as the source of a red dye for textiles.
A caravel was a small, highly manoeuvrable sailing ship developed by the Portuguese in the fifteenth century, often with lateen sails that allowed it to sail close to the wind.
A carrack was a large, three- or four-masted ocean-going sailing ship developed in the Mediterranean and Iberia in the fifteenth century.
Classical Greece is the period of ancient Greek history from the Persian Wars of the early fifth century BCE to the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE.
The Congreve rocket was a British military rocket developed by William Congreve in the early nineteenth century, based on rockets used in Mysore.
A counterweight trebuchet is a siege engine that uses a heavy falling weight to swing a throwing arm, capable of hurling large stones over long distances.
Danegeld was a tax raised in Anglo-Saxon England to pay tribute to Viking raiders, above all from 991 under Æthelred the Unready, when large sums were paid to Danish armies to stop their attacks.
Dry-stone construction is a building technique in which walls are made from carefully fitted stones without mortar.
A fortified camp is a defended encampment built by an army on campaign.
The Galilean moons are the four largest moons of Jupiter, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, discovered by Galileo Galilei with his telescope in January 1610.
A Gauleiter was the Nazi Party's leader of a regional branch, or Gau, in Germany and later in annexed territories.
Ge'ez is an ancient Semitic language of Ethiopia and Eritrea, with its own script.

Hanyu Pinyin is the official system for writing Standard Mandarin Chinese in the Latin alphabet, adopted by the People's Republic of China in 1958 and developed by a committee that included the linguist Zhou Youguang.
Iron smelting is the extraction of iron from ore by heating it in a furnace.
The magnetic compass is a navigational instrument that uses a magnetised needle to indicate direction.
Maharana, 'great rana', was the royal title of the rulers of Mewar, whose capital was Chittor and from 1559 Udaipur, and of a few other Rajput states such as Porbandar.
The Maxim gun was the first fully automatic machine gun, invented by Hiram Maxim in the 1880s.
A national debt is the total borrowing of a state, typically funded through government bonds.
Old French is the form of the French language spoken from around the ninth to the fourteenth century.
Old Javanese, or Kawi, is the literary and administrative language of Java recorded from the late 8th century, heavily influenced by Sanskrit.
Portuguese is a Romance language that originated in the western Iberian Peninsula.
The solidus was a gold coin introduced by the Roman emperor Constantine in the early fourth century.
Standard Chinese, or Standard Mandarin, is the official language of the People's Republic of China, based on the pronunciation of Beijing and the grammar of modern vernacular Mandarin literature.
Transhumance is the seasonal movement of livestock and herders between different pastures, typically between lowland winter grazing and highland summer grazing.
The trebuchet is a siege engine that uses a pivoting arm to hurl heavy projectiles, either by human traction or by a heavy counterweight.
Yavana is a term used in ancient Indian languages for Greeks and, later, for other westerners.
Zaju is a form of Chinese drama combining spoken dialogue, song and music, which reached its classical form under the Yuan Dynasty.
A chinampa is an artificial agricultural plot built up from mud and vegetation in shallow lake beds, separated by canals.
The Crown Dependencies are the Bailiwick of Jersey, the Bailiwick of Guernsey and the Isle of Man, self-governing possessions of the British Crown.
The feigned retreat is a tactic in which an army pretends to flee in order to draw the enemy into breaking formation, then turns to attack.
The First Intermediate Period is the era of ancient Egyptian history between the collapse of the Old Kingdom and the reunification of the country in the Middle Kingdom.
The Kipchak languages are a branch of the Turkic languages spoken from eastern Europe to Central Asia, including Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Tatar, Bashkir, Karakalpak, Nogai and Crimean Tatar.
The La Tène culture was the late Iron Age culture of Celtic Europe, from about 450 BCE until the Roman conquest.
The Mesoamerican Long Count calendar counts the days elapsed since a fixed starting date in 3114 BCE, using units based on twenty.
Old High German is the earliest recorded stage of the German language, used from about the eighth to the eleventh century.
Old Nubian is the medieval written form of the Nubian language, used in the Christian kingdoms of the middle Nile from about the 8th to the 15th century.
The pound sterling is the currency of the United Kingdom.
The Stato da Mar ('State of the Sea') was the collective name for the overseas possessions of the Republic of Venice, as distinct from its Italian mainland territories, the Domini di Terraferma.
The Tai Tham script, also called the Lanna script, is a writing system derived from the Mon script and used since about the 14th century for Northern Thai, Tai Lue, Tai Khün and Lao religious texts.
Tigrinya is a Semitic language of the Horn of Africa, spoken in the highlands of Eritrea and in the Tigray region of Ethiopia.
Amharic is a Semitic language of Ethiopia, written in the Ge'ez script, and the working language of the Ethiopian federal government.
Bronze-working is the craft of producing tools, weapons and ornaments from bronze, an alloy of copper and tin.
Cape Dutch was the form of Dutch spoken at the Cape of Good Hope by settlers, the enslaved and Khoekhoe communities from the 17th century.
Chemical weapons are toxic substances used in war to kill or injure, such as mustard gas.
Devanagari is an Indian script, written from left to right with a characteristic horizontal headline, in which each consonant carries an inherent vowel.
Dhu Raydan, after Raydan, the royal palace at the Himyarite capital Zafar, was the name by which the Himyarite kingdom of south Arabia appears in its inscriptions.
Earl of Clanricarde is a title in the Peerage of Ireland created in 1543 for Ulick na gCeann Burke, chief of the Burkes of south County Galway, under Henry VIII's policy of surrender and regrant.

Führer, German for 'leader', was the title used by Adolf Hitler as head of the Nazi Party and, from August 1934, as head of the German state after he merged the offices of president and chancellor on the death of Paul von Hindenburg.
Gandhari is a Middle Indo-Aryan language, or Prakrit, of the ancient region of Gandhara in what is now north-western Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan.
A kurgan is a burial mound raised over a grave, a form of tomb common across the Eurasian steppe from prehistoric times.
Lepontic is an ancient Celtic language known from about 140 inscriptions found around the Italian lakes and the southern Alps, dated from about the 6th to the 1st century BCE.
Linear Elamite is an ancient script used in Elam in the late third millennium BCE.
Litunga, meaning 'keeper of the earth', is the title of the king of the Lozi people of Barotseland in western Zambia.
Ndlovukati, meaning she-elephant, is the title of the queen mother of the Swazi Kingdom (Eswatini).

The Neopalatial or New Palace period is the high point of Minoan civilisation on Crete, from about 1700 to 1450 BCE, when the palaces of Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros were rebuilt on a grander scale and Minoan art, trade and…
Ngwenyama, meaning lion, is the title of the king of the Swazi Kingdom (Eswatini).
Odia, formerly spelled Oriya, is an Indo-Aryan language spoken mainly in Odisha, India, written in its own rounded script.
Old Malay is the earliest attested form of the Malay language, known from inscriptions in Sumatra and nearby regions.
Overgrazing occurs when livestock graze pasture more heavily than it can recover, degrading the land.
The Pallava script is a Brahmic script that developed in southern India under the Pallava dynasty from around the 4th century CE.
Papiamento is a creole language spoken on Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao in the southern Caribbean.

Ramlila is a dramatic re-enactment of the life of the god Rama, based on the Ramayana and especially Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, performed across northern India in the weeks around the Dussehra festival.
The San Pedro cactus, Echinopsis pachanoi, is a fast-growing columnar cactus native to the Andes of Peru and Ecuador.
Seven Wonders of the Ancient World

The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World are a list of remarkable monuments drawn up by Greek writers of the Hellenistic period: the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, the statue of Zeus at Olympia, the Temple of Artemis…
The Sharif of Mecca was the ruler of Mecca and much of the Hejaz, chosen from among the descendants of the Prophet Muhammad through his grandson Hasan, from the 10th century until 1925.
A siege tower is a mobile wooden tower used to bring attackers to the top of fortification walls.
Tenancy is an arrangement in which cultivators farm land owned by others in return for rent, labour or a share of the harvest.
The Uruk period is the archaeological period of Mesopotamia from about 4000 to 3100 BCE, named after the city of Uruk.
Agent Orange was a herbicide sprayed by the United States military over forests and crops in South Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia during the Vietnam War, mainly between 1962 and 1971.
An aircraft carrier is a warship designed to carry, launch and recover aircraft, serving as a mobile air base at sea.
The Ankole-Watusi is a breed of cattle known for its enormous horns, developed in the United States in the twentieth century from long-horned Sanga cattle of east-central Africa.
Asomtavruli is the oldest form of the Georgian alphabet, written with rounded letters.
A bicameral legislature is a lawmaking body divided into two separate chambers or houses.
The Black Ships was the Japanese name for the Western vessels, especially the steam-powered warships of Commodore Matthew Perry's American squadron that entered Edo Bay in 1853.
The Blue Riband is an unofficial honour given to the passenger liner making the fastest regular crossing of the Atlantic.
The Bren light machine gun was the standard light machine gun of the British and Commonwealth armies in the Second World War.
Bronze casting is the technique of shaping objects by pouring molten copper alloy into moulds, often using the lost-wax method.

Bull-leaping is an acrobatic feat in which a performer vaults over a charging bull, shown above all in the art of Minoan Crete, where it is thought to have been a key ritual of the elite and perhaps of religion.
Camel warfare refers to the use of camels in combat, for transport of troops and supplies or as mounts.
Cataract surgery is the treatment of the clouding of the eye's lens.
The CFA franc is the name of two currencies used in West and Central Africa, created by France in December 1945 for its African colonies.
Chagatai is an extinct Turkic literary language of Central Asia, named after the Chagatai Khanate.
Chain mail is armour made of small interlocking metal rings.
Chao was the paper currency issued by the Yuan Dynasty in China.
Chernozem, or black earth, is a highly fertile dark soil rich in humus, found across the steppes of Ukraine and southern Russia.
Copper ingots are cast bars or shapes of copper used for trade and storage of value.
The Coptic Pope of Alexandria is the patriarch and head of the Coptic Orthodox Church, the Miaphysite church of Egypt that separated from the Chalcedonian church after 451.
The Cross of Lorraine is a cross with two horizontal bars, originally the Cross of Anjou, which René II brought into use as an emblem of the dukes of Lorraine in the later fifteenth century.
Crucifixion is a method of execution in which the condemned is fastened to a cross or stake and left to die.
The daric was a gold coin of the Achaemenid Empire, introduced under Darius I.
Dauphin of France was the title of the heir apparent to the French throne from 1350 to 1830.
Elamite is the extinct language of ancient Elam, written first in its own scripts and later in cuneiform.
The Erligang culture is a Bronze Age culture of China dated to about 1600–1400 BCE, named after a site at Zhengzhou in Henan.
A fatwa is a formal legal opinion issued by a qualified Islamic jurist.
Federalism is a system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and constituent units.
A fire arrow was an arrow carrying an incendiary or gunpowder charge.
The First Sea Lord is the professional head of the British Royal Navy and the senior naval officer on the Admiralty Board.
Fon is the title of the sacred kings of the chiefdoms and kingdoms of the Cameroon Grassfields, such as Nso, Bafut and Bali-Nyonga.
The Four Asian Tigers are Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan, economies that industrialised rapidly from the 1960s to the 1990s.
God's Wife of Amun was the title of the highest-ranking priestess of the god Amun at Thebes.
The Gonfaloniere of Justice was the highest office of the Republic of Florence, created by the Ordinances of Justice of 1293 to command a militia enforcing the laws against the magnates.
The Gosanke, the 'three honourable houses', were the three senior branch families of the Tokugawa, founded by sons of Tokugawa Ieyasu: the Owari, Kii and Mito houses.
The Grantha script is a South Indian script derived from Brahmi, used from Pallava times to write Sanskrit in the Tamil country, where the Tamil script lacked letters for many Sanskrit sounds.
Groundwater depletion is the exhaustion of underground water reserves when extraction exceeds natural recharge.
Haiku is a short form of Japanese poetry, traditionally of three phrases following a five-seven-five syllable pattern and often evoking nature and the seasons.
Haitian Creole is a French-based creole language spoken by almost the whole population of Haiti.
The Hallstatt culture was the main archaeological culture of western and central Europe in the early Iron Age, from about 800 to 450 BCE, and is commonly associated with speakers of Proto-Celtic.
The hand cannon was an early firearm consisting of a simple metal tube fired by igniting gunpowder by hand.
HIV/AIDS is the disease caused by the human immunodeficiency virus, which weakens the immune system and, untreated, leads to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
The Indus script, also called the Harappan script, is the set of signs used by the Indus Valley Civilisation, found chiefly on stamp seals, seal impressions and pottery.
An ironclad was a steam-powered warship protected by iron or steel armour plates, developed in the mid-nineteenth century.
An iwan is a vaulted hall or space, walled on three sides and open on one, characteristic of Persian and Islamic architecture.
The Japanese tea ceremony is a ritual preparation and serving of powdered green tea, shaped by Zen Buddhist ideals of simplicity and harmony.
Jèrriais is the Norman language of Jersey, a variety of Norman French spoken on the island since the Middle Ages.
The Jersey Royal is a variety of early new potato grown in Jersey, developed around 1880 by the farmer Hugh de la Haye from an unusually large potato with many eyes.
Kabuki is a form of Japanese theatre combining drama, music and dance, known for stylised acting and elaborate costumes.
Kenjutsu is the Japanese art of swordsmanship.
Kente cloth is a brightly coloured woven textile of the Akan peoples of present-day Ghana, made from interwoven strips of cloth.
The Kilo class is the NATO name for a type of diesel-electric attack submarine designed in the Soviet Union and built from the early 1980s, later in an improved version known as Project 636.
A kiva is a room used by the Pueblo peoples of the American South-West for rites and political meetings; among the Hopi and most other Pueblos it is a round, underground chamber.
Kongo, or Kikongo, is a Bantu language spoken by the Kongo people in western Democratic Republic of the Congo, northern Angola and the Republic of the Congo.

Lachit Divas is an annual day of commemoration held in Assam, India, on 24 November, the birthday of Lachit Borphukan, the Ahom general who defeated the Mughal army at the Battle of Saraighat in 1671.
Landammann is the title of the chief magistrate in several Swiss cantons.
The Lex Rhodia was the maritime law of Rhodes on jettison: when cargo was thrown overboard to save a ship, the loss was shared among all whose property had been saved.
The Libyco-Berber script is an ancient alphabet of consonants used to write Berber languages across North Africa and the Canary Islands from at least the third century BCE.
Luxembourgish is a West Germanic language, derived from Moselle Franconian dialects, spoken as a mother tongue by most Luxembourgers.
Manuscript illumination is the decoration of handwritten books with painted images, ornament and gold.
Medism was the Greek term for collaborating with or siding with the Persian Empire, whose people the Greeks often called Medes.
The Minie rifle was a muzzle-loading rifled musket firing a conical bullet that expanded into the barrel's rifling, allowing accurate long-range fire.
Minnesang was the tradition of courtly love poetry and song in medieval Germany, flourishing from the twelfth to the fourteenth century.
Movable type is a printing system using individual, reusable characters that can be arranged to form texts.
Muqarnas is a form of architectural ornament in Islamic architecture consisting of tiers of small niches, creating a honeycomb or stalactite effect in vaults and domes.
Norman architecture is the Romanesque style of building developed in Normandy in the eleventh century and carried to England after 1066 and to southern Italy and Sicily.
The North African elephant was a population of elephants, now extinct, that lived in north-western Africa in antiquity.
Northern Black Polished Ware is a fine, glossy black or grey pottery of the Iron Age in northern India, made from about 700 to 200 BCE.
Northern Thai, known to its speakers as Kham Mueang, is the Tai language of the former kingdom of Lan Na, spoken by several million people in northern Thailand.
The Osco-Umbrian languages, also called Sabellic, are a group of extinct Italic languages once spoken across central and southern Italy.
Ostracism was an Athenian procedure by which the Assembly could exile a leading citizen for ten years without loss of property, by writing his name on potsherds, ostraka.
Papermaking is the craft of producing paper from plant fibres, invented in China.
The Parthian shot was a mounted archery tactic in which a horse archer, real or feigning retreat, turned in the saddle to shoot at pursuing enemies.
The Persian carpet is a hand-knotted rug made in Iran, part of a weaving tradition stretching back many centuries.
Persian is an Iranian language spoken mainly in Iran, Afghanistan and Tajikistan, whose literary form developed after the Islamic conquest from earlier Middle Persian.
The ʼPhags-pa script is an alphabet created by the Tibetan lama Drogön Chögyal Phagpa at the request of Kublai Khan.
Poison gas is a chemical weapon that injures or kills by inhalation or contact.
Polonisation is the adoption of the Polish language, culture and often Catholic religion by non-Polish groups.
The Porfiriato was the period of Porfirio Díaz's rule in Mexico, from 1876 to 1911, with an interval from 1880 to 1884.
The prefect of Egypt (praefectus Aegypti) was the governor of the Roman province of Egypt from its annexation in 30 BCE.
A protective tariff is a tax on imported goods designed to shield domestic producers from foreign competition.
The Rector of Ragusa was the nominal head of state of the Republic of Ragusa (Dubrovnik) from 1358 to 1808.
The rupee is a currency unit of the Indian subcontinent, descended from the silver rupiya coin introduced in the sixteenth century and later standardised under Mughal rule.
Salinisation is the build-up of salts in soil, often caused by long-term irrigation in hot, dry climates where evaporation leaves mineral deposits behind.
Sancai, meaning three colours, is a type of Chinese lead-glazed pottery decorated mainly in amber, green and cream, which flourished under the Tang Dynasty.
Sinhala is the Indo-Aryan language of the Sinhalese people and one of the official languages of Sri Lanka, written in its own script.
Soil erosion is the loss of the fertile top layer of soil through the action of water, wind or overuse.
Son of Heaven (tianzi) was a title of the Chinese ruler, first used by the kings of the Western Zhou, expressing the idea that the ruler held a mandate from Heaven to govern all under Heaven.
A sovereign default is a failure by a government to repay its debts.

Sranan Tongo is an English-based creole language that arose among enslaved Africans in Suriname in the seventeenth century, during the English period of the colony, and later absorbed many Dutch and Portuguese words.
A star catalogue is a list of stars with their positions and brightness.
The Sumerian language was the language of ancient Sumer, one of the earliest written languages.
A sumptuary law is a law that restricts consumption, such as clothing or luxury goods, often according to social rank.
The triangular trade was the Atlantic commercial system linking Europe, West Africa and the Americas from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries.
The tsetse fly is a blood-feeding insect of tropical Africa that transmits trypanosomiasis, a disease fatal to horses and cattle.
Typhus is a group of bacterial infectious diseases, often spread by lice, that cause fever and can be highly fatal in crowded or wartime conditions.
Ukiyo-e, meaning 'pictures of the floating world', is a genre of Japanese woodblock prints and paintings that flourished from the seventeenth to the nineteenth centuries.
The Vietnamese alphabet, chữ Quốc ngữ, is the Latin-based script used to write Vietnamese, with diacritics marking tones and vowels.
The Volga trade route was a network of river and portage routes linking Scandinavia and the Baltic with the Caspian Sea and the Islamic world via the Volga River in the early medieval period.
War reparations are payments imposed on a defeated state to compensate the victors for the costs and damage of war.
Weser Renaissance is the style of Renaissance architecture in the Weser region of north-western Germany, flourishing from about 1520 to 1620.
Woodblock printing is a technique of printing text or images by carving them in relief on a wooden block, inking it and pressing paper onto it.
Xing ware is a type of white porcelain produced at kilns in northern China under the Tang Dynasty.
The Zamorin, in Malayalam Samoothiri, was the title of the Hindu rulers of the Kingdom of Calicut on the Malabar Coast of Kerala from about the 12th century to 1766.
The ZB vz. 26 was a light machine gun designed by Václav Holek at the Zbrojovka Brno arms works and adopted by the Czechoslovak army in 1926.
Alanic was the Eastern Iranian language of the Alans, a nomadic people of the steppes north of the Caucasus in late antiquity and the Middle Ages.
Antillean Creole is a French-based creole language spoken in the Lesser Antilles, including Martinique, Guadeloupe, Dominica and Saint Lucia, where it is called Kwéyòl.
Burushaski is a language spoken in the Hunza, Nagar and Yasin valleys of Gilgit-Baltistan in northern Pakistan.
A cadastral survey is a systematic record of land parcels, recording their area, ownership, use and value, usually for taxation.
Chhau is a tradition of martial and folk dance from eastern India, performed in three main styles, Purulia in West Bengal, Seraikela in Jharkhand and Mayurbhanj in Odisha.
The corvus was a boarding bridge with a spike at its end, used by the Roman navy during the First Punic War.

Coyotlatelco is a style of red-on-buff pottery, and by extension the archaeological culture associated with it, found in the Basin of Mexico in the centuries after the decline of Teotihuacan, roughly 600 to 900 CE.
The Deutsche Mark was the currency of West Germany from June 1948 and of reunified Germany from 1990 until it was replaced by the euro in 2002.
The Đông Sơn culture was a Bronze Age culture of the Red River and Ma River valleys of northern Vietnam, named after a village in Thanh Hóa province.
Duke of Atholl is a title in the peerage of Scotland created in 1703 for John Murray, Marquess of Atholl.
Etsu Nupe is the title of the traditional ruler of the Nupe people of central Nigeria.
Grand Župan was the title of the supreme ruler of several early medieval South Slavic states, above the župans who governed individual districts.
The Green Corn Ceremony is the most important annual festival of the Muscogee (Creek), Seminole and other peoples of the south-eastern woodlands of North America.
Gross domestic product (GDP) is a measure of the total value of goods and services produced within an economy over a given period.
Gutsherrschaft is the German term for the manorial system that developed east of the Elbe from the 15th and 16th centuries.
The High King of Ireland, Ard Rí in Irish, was the title claimed by kings who asserted supremacy over the island's many kingdoms.
Hindko is a group of Indo-Aryan dialects spoken in north-western Pakistan, especially in the Hazara region and the city of Peshawar in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and in parts of northern Punjab.
A kopje is a small, isolated hill, often a rocky granite outcrop, rising from the surrounding plain in southern Africa.
Lavelua is the title of the paramount king of Uvea, or Wallis Island, in the Pacific.
A madhab is a school of Islamic jurisprudence, a tradition of legal interpretation based on the Quran and Sunna.
Magyarisation was the policy of spreading the Hungarian language and identity among the non-Hungarian peoples of the Kingdom of Hungary, pursued especially after the Compromise of 1867.
The Malayalam language is a Dravidian language spoken mainly in Kerala and Lakshadweep in south-western India, by about 35 million people.
Manx is a Goidelic Celtic language of the Isle of Man, closely related to Irish and Scottish Gaelic.
Nepal Sambat is a lunar calendar era of Nepal that begins in 879 CE.
Old Mon is the earliest recorded form of the Mon language, an Austroasiatic language of mainland Southeast Asia.
Penal transportation was the punishment of sending convicted criminals to a distant colony.

Prince of Transylvania was the title of the rulers of the Principality of Transylvania, first taken by John Sigismund Zápolya when he gave up the Hungarian royal title at the Treaty of Speyer in 1570.
Raffia cloth is a textile woven from the fibres of the raffia palm, produced in Central Africa.
Rajah of Sarawak was the title of the Brooke family, the 'White Rajahs', who ruled Sarawak in northern Borneo from 1841 to 1946.
Shudra is the fourth of the four varnas, the classes of traditional Hindu society described in Vedic and later Sanskrit texts, below the Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas.

The special administrative regions of China are Hong Kong and Macau, created under the principle of 'one country, two systems' when Britain returned Hong Kong in 1997 and Portugal returned Macau in 1999.
The states of Germany, or Länder, are the sixteen federated states of the Federal Republic of Germany, each with its own constitution, parliament and government.
Tagalog is an Austronesian language of the central Philippines, spoken natively around Manila and in southern Luzon.
Tamil-Brahmi is a variant of the Brahmi script used to write the Tamil language from around the 3rd or 2nd century BCE.
Tibeto-Burman is the name for the large group of Sino-Tibetan languages other than Chinese, spoken from the Himalayas to Myanmar and south-western China.
A villa, in the Carolingian context, was a great landed estate belonging to the church, the crown or the aristocracy.
An aqueduct is a channel or structure built to carry water from a source to a city, often across valleys on arches.
The Arawakan languages are a family of languages of South America and the Caribbean, spoken from the Andes and Amazonia to the Antilles.

The Associates of the Swiss Confederacy, in German zugewandte Orte, were territories allied to the Old Swiss Confederacy without being full member cantons.
Balochi is an Iranian language spoken by the Baloch people in Pakistan's Balochistan province, south-eastern Iran, southern Afghanistan and among communities in Oman and the Gulf.
Biatec is a name, probably that of a Celtic ruler, inscribed on large silver coins minted in the 1st century BCE at the oppidum on the site of modern Bratislava, in the lands of the Boii.
The Bonnie Blue Flag is a flag of a single white star on a blue field, first flown by the short-lived Republic of West Florida in 1810.
A broch is a type of Iron Age drystone tower found in northern and western Scotland, especially in Caithness, Orkney and Shetland.
Cape Verdean Creole, known as Kriolu, is a Portuguese-based creole language spoken in Cape Verde and by its emigrant communities.
Cipollino is a green-and-white banded marble quarried in antiquity near Karystos in southern Euboea, Greece.

The cog was a type of sailing ship used in northern Europe from the 10th to the 14th century, with a flat bottom, high straight sides, a single square sail and, later, a stern rudder and raised castles.
The Companions of the Prophet, in Arabic sahaba, are the people who knew or saw the Prophet Muhammad and believed in him.
Cumbric was the Brittonic Celtic language of the early medieval north of Britain, spoken in the kingdom of Strathclyde and in Cumbria.
Cyfraith Hywel, the law of Hywel, was the native law of medieval Wales, traditionally said to have been codified under Hywel Dda in the 10th century.
The Cypro-Minoan syllabary is an undeciphered script used on Cyprus in the Late Bronze Age, from about 1550 to 1050 BCE.
Cyzicenes were electrum coins struck by the Greek city of Cyzicus on the Sea of Marmara from the 6th to the 4th century BCE.
Damel was the title of the kings of Cayor, a Wolof kingdom on the coast of Senegal.
The Dharmachakra, or Wheel of the Law, is a Buddhist symbol representing the teaching of the Buddha, recalling his first sermon at Sarnath, known as setting the wheel of the Dharma in motion.

Druk Gyalpo, 'Dragon King', is the title of the head of state of Bhutan.
Duke of Aveiro was a Portuguese ducal title created in 1535 for João de Lencastre, a grandson of King John II.
The Early Minoan period is the first phase of the Bronze Age Minoan civilisation of Crete, from about 3100 to 2100 BCE.

Eid al-Ghadir is a Shia Muslim festival held on 18 Dhu al-Hijja to commemorate the Prophet Muhammad's sermon at Ghadir Khumm in 632, in which Shia Muslims see the designation of Ali ibn Abi Talib as his successor.
Esperanto is a constructed international language created by the Polish ophthalmologist L. L. Zamenhof and first published in 1887.
Eteocypriot is the name given to a non-Greek language of ancient Cyprus, known from inscriptions written in the Cypriot syllabary between about the 8th and 4th centuries BCE.
Galician-Portuguese was the Romance language of medieval Galicia and northern Portugal, from which modern Galician and Portuguese developed.
Ganjifa is a family of card games played with round, hand-painted cards, introduced to India from Persia and popular at the Mughal court in the 16th century.
The Gatling gun is a hand-cranked, rapid-firing gun with several rotating barrels, patented by the American inventor Richard Gatling in 1862.
The Gbe languages are a group of closely related languages of the Volta–Niger family spoken from south-eastern Ghana through Togo and Benin to south-western Nigeria.
Germanisation is the spread of the German language, people and culture into other lands, through settlement or state policy.
Gorani is a Northwestern Iranian language spoken in parts of the Zagros on both sides of the Iran–Iraq border, closely related to Zazaki.

Grenzer were the soldier-settlers of the Habsburg Military Frontier, the border zone against the Ottoman Empire in Croatia, Slavonia, Hungary and later Transylvania.
Guarani is a Tupi–Guarani language of South America and one of the two official languages of Paraguay, alongside Spanish, spoken by most Paraguayans regardless of background.
Hadramautic was one of the Ancient South Arabian languages, written in the Kingdom of Hadramawt in what is now eastern Yemen from the early first millennium BCE until about the 4th century CE.
Hattic was the language of the Hattians of central Anatolia in the 3rd and early 2nd millennium BCE.
The Heller was a German coin first struck at the imperial mint of Schwäbisch Hall in the 12th century as a silver pfennig, the Haller pfennig, from which its name comes.
The Hindu–Arabic numeral system is the decimal place-value system of writing numbers with ten digits, including zero, used throughout the world today.
The Iroquoian languages are a family of Native American languages of eastern North America.
The Je Khenpo is the chief abbot of the Central Monastic Body of Bhutan and the country's highest religious authority.
Kapudan Pasha was the title of the grand admiral of the Ottoman navy, from the 16th century one of the highest officials of the empire.
The Karmapa is the head of the Karma Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism and the oldest line of reincarnated lamas in Tibet, beginning with Düsum Khyenpa in the 12th century.
Khowar, also called Chitrali, is an Indo-Aryan language of the Dardic group spoken by several hundred thousand people in Chitral in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, and in parts of Gilgit-Baltistan.
Kyabazinga is the title of the king of Busoga, in eastern Uganda.
The Late Classic is the period of Maya history from about 600 to 900 CE, when lowland Maya civilisation reached its height.
Llanito is the vernacular speech of Gibraltar, an Andalusian Spanish base mixed heavily with British English through frequent code-switching.
Lord of Mann is the title of the ruler of the Isle of Man.
Lord of the Isles, in Latin Dominus Insularum, was the title of the Clan Donald rulers of the Hebrides and western Highlands, first used by John of Islay in 1336.
Maltese is the national language of Malta and an official language of the European Union.

Mandarin Chinese is the largest group of Chinese dialects, spoken across northern and south-western China, and the basis of Standard Chinese, the official language of the People's Republic of China and Taiwan.
Mawlid is the celebration of the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad, held by many Muslims on 12 Rabi al-Awwal, the third month of the Islamic calendar.
Mehri is a Modern South Arabian language spoken by the Mahra people of eastern Yemen and western Oman, and by migrants in the Gulf states.
Messapic was an extinct Indo-European language of the Messapians of south-eastern Italy, in the Salento peninsula of Apulia.

Niçard, or Nissart, is the variety of Occitan traditionally spoken in Nice and its former county, usually classed as a sub-dialect of Provençal.
Ninja, or shinobi, were warriors of pre-modern Japan who specialised in espionage, scouting, infiltration and surprise attacks, especially in the Sengoku period of the 15th and 16th centuries.

The Oba of Lagos is the traditional ruler of Lagos, Nigeria.
Old Khmer is the earliest recorded form of the Khmer language, used in inscriptions in Cambodia from the seventh century.
The Olowo is the title of the king of Owo, a Yoruba kingdom in Ondo State, Nigeria.
The Olu of Warri is the title of the king of the Itsekiri people of the western Niger Delta in Nigeria.
Onojie, plural Enijie, is the title of the hereditary traditional rulers of the Esan chiefdoms in Edo State, Nigeria.
Osmanya is an alphabet for the Somali language created around 1920 by Osman Yusuf Kenadid, son of the sultan of Hobyo.
The Oto-Manguean languages are a large family of Indigenous languages of Mexico and Central America, including Zapotec, Mixtec, Otomi, Mazahua and Chinantec.
The Painted Grey Ware culture is an Iron Age archaeological culture of the western Ganges plain and the Ghaggar-Hakra valley in northern India, dated to roughly 1200–600 BCE.

Riau Malay is the variety of Malay spoken in the Riau archipelago and the old Johor-Riau sultanate.
Sadeh is an ancient Iranian festival celebrated with great bonfires fifty days before Nowruz, at the end of January, to honour fire and mark the waning of winter.
Shina is a Dardic Indo-Aryan language spoken in Gilgit-Baltistan in northern Pakistan and in neighbouring parts of Kashmir and Kohistan.
Sidetic was an Anatolian language spoken at Side on the Pamphylian coast of southern Turkey, related to Luwian and Lycian.
Soqotri is a Modern South Arabian language spoken on Socotra and its neighbouring islands, part of Yemen.

The Supreme Leader of Iran is the highest office of the Islamic Republic of Iran, created by the constitution of 1979 on the principle of the guardianship of the Islamic jurist.
Tetum is an Austronesian language of the island of Timor and, with Portuguese, one of the two official languages of Timor-Leste.

Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre was the title taken by Godfrey of Bouillon after the crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099, when he declined to be called king.

The Canadian Red Ensign was a red flag with the Union Jack in the canton and the Canadian coat of arms in the fly, used as Canada's unofficial and later official national flag on land and at sea from the late nineteenth century.
Chữ Nôm is a script for writing the Vietnamese language, built from Chinese characters and new characters formed on their model.

The Javanese calendar was introduced by Sultan Agung of Mataram in 1633.

A people's commissar was a minister of the Soviet government between 1917 and 1946, a member of the Council of People's Commissars in charge of a branch of administration such as war, foreign affairs or nationalities.

The Protogeometric style is the style of Greek pottery of about 1050–900 BCE, after the collapse of Mycenaean civilisation, decorated with concentric circles and semicircles drawn with compasses and multiple brushes.
